one_liner: Monotone bucket-based radix heap for Rust; ~1.7-2x faster than std BinaryHeap<Reverse<u32>> for large random u32 heapsort.
what_it_does: RadixHeap<K, V> is a generic monotone priority queue: push/pop/peek_key over key-value pairs, restricted to workloads where popped keys never decrease (e.g. Dijkstra). It is a separate crate type, not a drop-in for std::collections::BinaryHeap -- different type name, no peek_mut/into_sorted_vec/iter/From<Vec>, and pushing a key smaller than the last popped key panics instead of being accepted. Keys must implement the crate's Key trait, which is pre-implemented for all fixed-width integer primitives (u8-u128, i8-i128, usize, isize) and f32/f64.
how_it_is_fast: Classic radix-heap bucketing: on push, the key is XORed with the last-extracted minimum and the position of the highest differing bit picks a bucket (RadixHeap::get_bucket_to_insert_into in src/heap.rs), so push is an O(1) append with no per-element comparisons against existing heap contents, unlike BinaryHeap's O(log n) sift. pop scans for the first nonempty bucket and, only when it isn't bucket 0, redistributes that bucket's elements into finer buckets (rearrange()) before returning the true minimum (tracked per-bucket via a real `<` comparison, not the XOR trick). For fixed-width integers the bit range is a small constant (e.g. 32 for u32), making amortized pop cost effectively O(1) in practice.
when_to_use: Dijkstra / SSSP or other monotone-extraction graph algorithms where extracted keys are non-decreasing
Fixed-width integer keys (u8-u128, i8-i128, usize/isize) or f32/f64, large N (millions), push-all-then-pop-all or monotone-interleaved throughput workloads
Rust code currently doing BinaryHeap<Reverse<K>> for a min-heap and able to change call sites, not just imports
Willing to accept a hard panic (not a Result) as the failure mode if a non-monotone key is ever pushed
OK vendoring a small (4-file), unaudited, non-1.0 crate rather than depending on a maintained package
when_not_to_use: General-purpose priority queue where later-pushed keys can be smaller than an already-popped minimum (this panics; BinaryHeap just works)
You need BinaryHeap's API surface: peek_mut, into_sorted_vec, iterator support, From<Vec>, etc. -- none exist here
Non-numeric or custom key types beyond what you're willing to hand-implement Key (xor + position_of_highest_set_bit) for yourself
Multi-threaded/concurrent access -- no Sync/Send or synchronization documented or present in source
Production reliance on correctness/maintenance guarantees: 0-star, two-author WS2023/24 university coursework crate with no releases

integration.dependencies: rand 0.8.5 (runtime); proptest 1.3.1 and criterion 0.5 (dev-only, for tests/benches)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition (Cargo.toml edition = "2021"); exact MSRV not documented
integration.platforms: not documented; pure safe Rust with no unsafe blocks, no SIMD intrinsics, and no arch-specific code observed in heap.rs, bucket.rs, or key.rs
integration.thread_safety: not documented -- no Sync/Send impls or synchronization in the source read
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- explain: same conceptual push/pop shape as BinaryHeap<Reverse<K>> but a distinct type with a smaller method set and an added monotonicity precondition BinaryHeap doesn't have, so call sites must change, not just the import

gotchas: push() panics with "Invalid Key" (not a Result/Option) if the key is smaller than the last-extracted minimum -- a crash risk if input isn't guaranteed monotone

f32/f64 support XORs raw IEEE-754 bit patterns via to_bits() with no separate sign-order transform; verified only by two fixed 5-element unit tests (f32, f64) -- the proptest random-key property test covers only u32, not floats
LICENSE file in the repo is Apache-2.0, while Cargo.toml and the README both declare MIT -- check which actually applies before vendoring
A compiled binary (src/main.exe) is committed to the repo alongside src/main.rs, suggesting light packaging/CI hygiene
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over prio_queue (rollbear) or pair_radix_heap when you're in Rust, not C++ (those are C++-only). Versus SimdQuickHeap, the other Rust sibling beating the same BinaryHeap baseline, SimdQuickHeap reports far larger per-element speedups (~12-14x, AVX2/AVX512) and isn't monotone-restricted, so prefer this crate only when you specifically want the simpler bucket/XOR radix-heap technique for a Dijkstra-style monotone workload without SIMD or nightly-feature requirements.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own Criterion benchmark (benches/benchmark.rs) pushes N random u32 keys then pops all of them (N = 125,000 << i, i in 0..10, i.e. 125K-64M) against std::collections::BinaryHeap<Reverse<u32>>, on an unspecified 'mid-range desktop CPU' with no compiler version or flags stated; reported totals: 1M ~180ms vs ~320ms, 8M ~1.6s vs ~3.0s, 64M ~15s vs ~28s (~1.7-2x faster).
status_note: Last commit 2026-05-14 (active by date) but is a two-author WS2023/24 university coursework project with 0 stars, 0 forks, and no tagged releases beyond Cargo.toml's 0.1.0; small and dependency-light enough to vendor, but treat as unaudited/unmaintained-risk rather than a supported package.
